before: As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would. You ask hard things of it so it can grow, at its own pace. That's what I was just asking of you, with that new interest. You also widen its world with art and music, and you point out beautiful things when you see them. Nature is part of that, and so is the wider world past the end of the street you grew up on.
after: The opposite trap is forced adulthood, where you demand perfect discipline of yourself and have no visible needs, and very little joy or closeness. If you're stuck there, the next adult act may be asking for help or saying what you'd prefer, instead of tightening control again. Either of those can feel like turning into the needy one. Once a need does show, judge the strategy as well as the need: wanting closeness is legitimate, and demanding instant replies or punishing someone for needing space isn't the same thing. The Guide helps you find a workable way to meet the need without erasing you or the other person.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Without direction, reparenting can become permissive. The child receives attention but doesn’t develop. Candy, screens, and escape from anything difficult can masquerade as self-love.
brief:
- without direction, reparenting can turn permissive (keep "can")
- the child gets attention but doesn't grow (the article already says a life of only caring for yourself becomes "a never-ending therapy session", so at most a short clause)
- candy, screens, and escaping anything difficult can pass for self-love (keep "can": candy and screens aren't condemned outright)
- context, not for the text: When the Urge to Escape Arrives says "I'd thank whatever part of you came up with the escape plan, and slow down." Don't shame escape urges; the point is escape passing itself off as self-love.
